Instagram page or website? Why your Instagram shop needs a website of its own
A shop that only has a page is built on rented land. This article is about the morning the lease ends.
21 November 2026·8 min read·The dadmor team

In this article

  1. A page is rented. Here is what that means
  2. Where DMs stop working
  3. When is a page honestly enough?
  4. The right model: page for attention, website for the till
  5. What a website for an Instagram shop actually means
  6. In short

Summary

  1. A page is rented attention: the audience, the rules and the road to your customer are not yours. A website is the one digital asset with your name on the deed.
  2. While sales are small and experimental, a page alone is honestly enough, and building a website is rushing.
  3. The right model is not choosing one: the page brings the customer, the website closes the sale and keeps it.
It is seven in the morning. You pick up your phone to answer last night’s orders. You open Instagram and instead of your shop page you see a message: this account is not available.

Three years of posts and stories, a few thousand followers, hundreds of customers whose only address is a username, and every open order sitting inside the DMs. None of it is in your hands. You have no customer list, no phone numbers, not even a note of who ordered what last night and whether they paid.

We are not telling this story to scare you, and it does not end with “so buy a website today”. This happens to real shops every week: sometimes a hack, sometimes a mistaken report, sometimes the owner’s own slip against a platform rule, sometimes no explanation at all. Some pages come back. Some do not. The point of this article is one sentence: know which part of your business stands on your own land and which part stands on rented land, then decide for yourself.
A page is rented. Here is what that means
Rent is not always paid in money. On Instagram you rent three things, and you pay for them in dependence:

items: Reach: how many people see your post is not your call. The algorithm loves one content format today and drops it tomorrow, and your sales ride along with its taste.
Audience: your followers are Instagram’s users, not your customers. There is no official way to take their list with you. If the account closes, the audience goes with it.
Rules: DM limits, link limits, ad formats, even which products may be sold, are set by the landlord and can change whenever the landlord likes.

blocks.html: A website is the reverse of all three. The domain is registered in your name. The pages and content are yours. Your customer list, with the phone numbers and emails customers gave you themselves, stays in your hands. If you dislike your hosting, you pick the site up and move it, and no customer gets lost on the way. The difference between a page and a website is not more buttons. It is ownership.
Where DMs stop working
Even if the page never disappears, selling through DMs has a ceiling, and most sellers hit it exactly when business gets good:

items: Orders get lost between dozens of chats, and tracking each one depends on your memory.
One repeated question, price and availability, gets answered by hand dozens of times a day.
A customer is ready to buy at 2 a.m. and you are asleep. By morning they bought from another page.
There are no orderly invoices or purchase history. If a parcel goes wrong, there is no record to settle the dispute.
Discounts, gift codes and sales cannot run in an orderly way, because there is no basket and no till.

blocks.html: None of this means the page is bad. It means your selling tool has become too small for your volume. DMs were built for starting, not for staying.
A customer you only have in your DMs is not your customer. They are the platform’s customer, and the platform can close your road to them whenever it wants.
When is a page honestly enough?

Honestly: not always. If you have just started and still do not know which product sells, if your monthly sales are small and DMs handle them comfortably, or if your catalogue is so small that one tidy highlight does all the work, building a website is still too early. Spend your money on product and content. We do not sell a website to anyone whose sales are not proven yet, because first it has to be clear what sells. Then you build it a home.

The signs that website time has arrived are usually one of these: you have lost an order. You have lost a customer only because you replied late. Answering messages is eating the hours that should go into product and content. Or customers keep asking you: do you not have a website?
The right model: page for attention, website for the till

In practice the winning combination is not a choice between the two. The page gets seen every day, talks and builds trust. The bio link takes the warmed up customer to that product’s page on your site. The purchase finishes on the site with a payment gateway, an invoice and an order number. Next time, you send the sale news yourself by SMS or email instead of waiting for the algorithm’s kindness.

A website also makes the page stronger. Site content feeds posts and stories. A product page is a ready made answer to every “how much is it?” DM: one link instead of ten messages back and forth. And if the page is one day limited or closed, sales do not sleep, because your regular customers know your home address and keep buying there until the page returns.
What a website for an Instagram shop actually means

A website for an Instagram shop is not a corporate site with a few extra buttons. It has minimums that come straight out of those DM pains: a tidy catalogue with real prices and stock, a product page that answers every repeated DM question on the spot, a payment gateway and order tracking, a buying and returns policy page that builds trust with new customers, and a clear two way connection between page and site.

Anything beyond these minimums needs a sales reason, or it is decorative cost and does not belong in the scope. If you want to see how these minimums get fixed on paper, our project scope article publishes the full template.
In short

A page is for being seen; a website is for selling and lasting. They are not rivals. Ask yourself one question: if my page is gone tomorrow morning, how many days of sales do I have? If the answer is zero, your problem is not only the missing website. It is a risk that grows every day, and a website is one of its answers. And if the honest answer is that there is not enough sales yet to lose, run the page with a clear mind and keep this article for its day.

Frequently asked questions
